title: Programmable design of synthetic plant immune receptors for pathogen protein recognition.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded the 20.4 MB Zenodo deposit (CC-BY-4.0) and unzipped it: 405 predicted-structure files in mmCIF format (a standard structure file), 18 pathogen-protein PDB structure files, one README, no data tables. I parsed all 405 structures myself: every one holds exactly 2 protein chains (pathogen protein + designed binder); binder chains are 71-147 amino acids long (median 103), 400 of 405 binder sequences are unique, mean per-residue confidence (pLDDT) 80.0-97.9. 391 files are original designs and 14 are evolved variants in two 'evo' folders, matching the paper's '391 SPIRs designed'. I also read the GitHub file tree (453 entries: 4 scripts, 1 FASTA sequence file, the structures) and downloaded the 70 KB analysis script - it contains only helper functions, no experimental results. science.org returned HTTP 403 for the article and for two guessed supplementary-file URLs; the paper is not in PubMed Central.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the experimental outcome: that 71 of 391 designs (18.2%) recognized their target and activated an immune response, the directed-evolution improvements, the specificity and stacking experiments, and the transgenic-plant resistance to tomato brown rugose fruit virus. These come from the abstract plus the Chinese Academy of Sciences press release and EurekAlert summary, not from any file I opened. No per-design outcome table was found anywhere public.

a1_downloadable.note: Two different things. The design inputs (391 predicted complexes, pathogen structures, sequences) download freely from Zenodo under CC-BY-4.0 - verified. The file that holds the measured outcomes is the Science supplementary material, and science.org returned HTTP 403 for both the article page and the supplementary-file URLs; the paper is subscription-only and absent from PubMed Central, so the label-bearing table is not retrievable.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL, and this is the decisive one. Nothing in the public deposit records whether a design worked. There is no results table, no activity column, no filename or folder flag separating the 71 successes from the 320 failures - I checked all 405 filenames and all 453 repository entries. The label would have to be reconstructed by reading cell-death photographs and gel panels out of the paper's figures, i.e. constructed, not read.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are genuinely present, not referenced: I extracted the binder amino-acid sequence and the pathogen-protein sequence from every one of the 405 structure files, plus per-residue confidence scores in the B-factor column. No accession lookups needed.

a4_units_stated.note: The intended label is a qualitative in-plant readout (visible cell death / immune activation scored from leaf images). No units, no scale, and no quantitative version of it exists in any accessible file.

a5_enough_rows.note: 391 designed receptors (verified by counting non-evo structure files), which sits just below the ~400 minimum for a classification task. Worse, the natural grouping unit for an honest split is the pathogen target: only 21 target folders and 24 unique pathogen-protein chains, so a held-out-target evaluation would have about 20 groups of ~8-48 designs each.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 20.4 MB zip, ~75 MB unpacked; the parsed sequence table I built is under 1 MB
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially laptop-sized; I parsed all 405 structures in well under a minute on CPU.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: 391 non-evo structure files exactly matches the paper's stated 391 designed receptors, so the design side is internally consistent. The 71 successes cannot be cross-checked against any file.

a8_label_provenance.note: The only per-design numbers that ARE public are the design pipeline's own confidence scores (AlphaFold/HelixFold3 interface predicted TM-score, predicted TM-score, pLDDT). Training on those would be distilling the model that generated the designs - textbook circularity - and they were used as the selection filter, so every design in the deposit already passed them.

existing_models.name: BindCraft (Pacesa et al., Nature 2025) - the de novo binder design pipeline this paper used to make its binders
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported experimental success rates of 10-100% depending on target; from the Nature abstract and the project wiki retrieved by search, not from reading the full paper.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Which designs will work experimentally is still decided by in-silico filters with imperfect precision; raw wet-lab hit rates before developability filtering are low.

existing_models.name: IARA, a graph neural network filter for bindable protein surfaces (bioRxiv 2026, 'A deep learning predictor of bindable protein surfaces to guide generative synthetic biology')
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on 1,067 successful BindCraft runs against synthetic targets; numbers taken from the search snippet only, I did not retrieve the paper.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Triaging generative binder pipelines before synthesis is explicitly still open.

existing_models.name: Computational design of de novo integrated domains for plant NLR immune receptors (bioRxiv 2026.07.10.737686) - direct competitor on the same engineering task
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved beyond the title; indicates at least one other group is doing designed integrated-decoy domains in plant immune receptors.

c2_audit.note: Searched because the field matters for whether the data would be worth chasing. Searching was partial: the evaluation stopped at the A2 failure, so this list is not exhaustive.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model with small CPU-runnable checkpoints) would have been the obvious backbone for binder sequences, with pLDDT/interface features as side inputs
backbone.hardware: laptop CPU: 405 sequences of ~100-200 amino acids embed in minutes
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; the deposit itself is CC-BY-4.0, so licensing was never the problem

integration.partner_dataset: Protein Data Bank / AlphaFold DB for the pathogen proteins; UniProt for coat-protein and effector sequences
integration.join_key: protein sequence or UniProt accession (the deposit gives sequences, not accessions, so a sequence search would be needed)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Not assessed further: without the per-design outcome label there is nothing to join a partner resource to.

controls.positive_control: Would have been available in principle - the paper includes known working receptor parts (Pikm-1 with its natural integrated domain, AVR-PikD) and the two evolved series - but with no outcome labels there is nothing to control.
controls.external_validation: The companion Science paper 'Systematic discovery and engineering of synthetic immune receptors in plants' (10.1126/science.adx2508) has an open Zenodo deposit (record 15468929) and would be the natural second source, but it was not inspected here.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible from the public files: they contain 391 designed receptor-pathogen complexes that all passed the same in-silico filters, with no record of which ones worked in a plant, so any model trained on them would only be re-predicting the filter that selected them.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a designed binder's sequence and predicted structure to predict whether the engineered plant immune receptor fires on its pathogen target.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one synthetic plant immune receptor: the designed binder's amino-acid sequence, the pathogen protein it targets, and their predicted complex structure with per-residue confidence. 391 such designs across 21 pathogen targets are public and I verified them.
plain_idea.predict: A yes/no: did the receptor recognize its target and trigger the plant's cell-death immune response when tested in leaves. The true answer comes from the authors' in-plant assays (visible cell death after transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana) - and it is exactly this answer that is missing from every public file.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Crop-protection and protein-design groups synthesize dozens of designs per target at real cost; a filter that raised the 18% hit rate would cut that directly. Even a failed model would tell us whether structure-prediction confidence scores carry any signal about in-plant function.

ml_idea: Intended idea: classify which of 391 synthetic plant immune receptors activate immunity, from the designed binder sequence plus the predicted binder-pathogen complex (frozen ESM-2 embeddings plus interface features, with pathogen target held out). Dead on arrival because the outcome column exists only inside the paywalled Science supplement and the paper's figures. The public deposit is the design pipeline's output, not its results.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not guessed, for the input side: the 20.4 MB zip unpacks to ~75 MB and I parsed all 405 structures to sequences in under a minute of CPU time. Embedding 405 short sequences with a small ESM-2 checkpoint would take minutes. Compute was never the constraint.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Grep the deposit for any outcome column - done in one command, and it killed the project: 405 mmCIF files, 18 PDB files, 1 FASTA, 4 scripts, 1 README, and not a single results table with an activity, cell-death or hit/miss field.

verdict_reason: A2 and A1 fail together: the public CC-BY deposit holds only the 391 designed receptor structures (all of which passed the same in-silico filter), while the measured outcome - which 71 worked in a plant - sits in Science supplementary material that returns HTTP 403 and is absent from PubMed Central, so the label would have to be read out of figure panels. A5 fails too at 391 rows across only ~21 pathogen targets, and the sole public per-design numbers are the design model's own confidence scores, which is A8 circularity. Worth re-checking in a year if the authors deposit the per-design assay table.
